pageProps.title: Flashing LineageOS 14.1 for Samsung Galaxy Note 8.0 (n5110)
pageProps.review: A detailed guide on flashing the custom-built LineageOS 14.1 ROM and recovery image to the Samsung Galaxy Note 8.0 (n5110) using the Heimdall tool in a Linux environment, including the device initialization process.
pageProps.description: A guide to flashing the compiled LineageOS 14.1 ROM and recovery image to the Samsung Galaxy Note 8.0 (n5110).
pageProps.content: ## Flashing LineageOS 14.1 for Samsung Galaxy Note 8.0 (n5110) In the previous post, we built the custom LineageOS 14.1 ROM and recovery image for the Samsung Galaxy Note 8.0 (n5110). In this post, we will cover the process of flashing the build outputs to the device and verifying its operation after booting. ### Flashing recovery.img using Heimdall While you can use `Odin` for flashing, I preferred using Heimdall as I like working in a Linux environment. Since the Heimdall package is already available in the Ubuntu repository, it can be easily installed using `apt`. ```sh { "title": "Install Heimdall in Ubuntu using apt" } --- $ sudo apt install heimdall-flash heimdall-flash-frontend ``` After installation, enter Download (Odin) mode by long-pressing the Power + Vol Down keys simultaneously. Connect via USB and check the device connection status using the `heimdall detect` command. ```sh { "title": "Check Heimdall connection" } --- $ heimdall detect Device detected ``` Once the device is correctly recognized by `Heimdall`, flash the `recovery.img` file using the `flash` command. ```sh { "title": "Flash recovery.img using Heimdall" } --- $ heimdall flash --RECOVERY ./out/target/product/n5110/recovery.img --no-reboot Heimdall v2.0.2 ... Initialising connection... Detecting device... Claiming interface... Initialising protocol... Resetting device... Protocol initialisation successful. ... // [!code highlight] Uploading RECOVERY 100% RECOVERY upload successful Ending session... Releasing device interface... ``` It seems the image has been successfully flashed. Now, enter Recovery Mode and install the custom ROM image. ```adcard ``` ### Enter Recovery Mode & Wipe With the recovery flashed, proceed to initialize the device to install the new custom ROM. 1. Enter recovery mode (Lineage Recovery) by pressing the Power + Vol Up + Home keys simultaneously. 2. Perform a Factory reset and wipe the Cache partition to clear existing data. 3. To install the ROM, select the Apply Update -> Apply from ADB menu to enter sideload mode. ```adcard ``` ### Setup udev Rules (for Linux) To use ADB Sideload in a Linux environment like Ubuntu, you may need to configure udev rules to assign appropriate permissions to the USB device. When you connect the device in Sideload mode to your PC, you can find logs like the following in `dmesg`. ```sh { "title": "dmesg output" } --- $ dmesg | tail [144461.822906] usb 1-2: new high-speed USB device number 12 using xhci_hcd // [!code highlight] [144461.947399] usb 1-2: New USB device found, idVendor=18d1, idProduct=d001, bcdDevice= 2.26 [144461.947412] usb 1-2: New USB device strings: Mfr=2, Product=3, SerialNumber=4 [144461.947417] usb 1-2: Product: GT-N5110 [144461.947421] usb 1-2: Manufacturer: samsung [144461.947425] usb 1-2: SerialNumber: 4103e10fb64b2161 ``` Use the Vendor ID (`18d1`) and Product ID (`d001`) identified above to create or modify the /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules file. Add the following content to grant USB device access permissions to the `plugdev` group. ```sh { "title": "Edit /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules" } --- $ sudo vi /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules // [!code word:18d1] // [!code word:d001] // [!code ++] SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="18d1", ATTR{idProduct}=="d001", MODE="0666", GROUP="plugdev" ``` After adding the entry, reload the udev rules and restart the service. ```sh { "title": "Reload udev rules" } --- $ sudo udevadm control --reload-rules $ sudo service udev restart ``` ### Flash LineageOS via ADB Sideload Now, restart the ADB server and check if the device is correctly recognized in `sideload` status. ```sh { "title": "Check ADB devices" } --- $ adb kill-server $ adb start-server $ adb devices List of devices attached 4103e10fb64b2161 sideload ``` If the device is correctly recognized as `sideload`, transfer the built `lineage-*.zip` file to the device to start the installation. ```sh { "title": "ADB Sideload" } --- $ adb sideload out/target/product/n5110/lineage-14.1-20260306-UNOFFICIAL-n5110.zip serving: 'lineage-14.1-20260306-UNOFFICIAL-n5110.zip' (100%) ... Total xfer: 1.00x ``` ### Verify Installation After the installation is complete, reboot the system (Reboot system now). You should see the Lineage OS logo as it boots up normally. Just like standard Android, you need to enable the Android debugging option in Developer Options for ADB connectivity. Also, set Root access to 'ADB only' to use root privileges in the ADB environment. When testing the `adb devices` command for ADB connection, the device might not be recognized. This is because the `idVendor` and `idProduct` values might have changed from those used in Sideload mode. ```sh { "title": "dmesg after reboot" } --- [145449.425869] usb 1-2: USB disconnect, device number 24 [145456.752554] usb 1-2: new high-speed USB device number 25 using xhci_hcd // [!code highlight] // [!code word:18d1] // [!code word:4ee7] [145456.876497] usb 1-2: New USB device found, idVendor=18d1, idProduct=4ee7, bcdDevice= 2.26 [145456.876512] usb 1-2: New USB device strings: Mfr=2, Product=3, SerialNumber=4 [145456.876517] usb 1-2: Product: GT-N5110 [145456.876521] usb 1-2: Manufacturer: samsung [145456.876525] usb 1-2: SerialNumber: 4103e10fb64b2161 ``` Just as we did before, add the newly changed `idVendor` and `idProduct` values to the udev rules. ```sh { "title": "Edit /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules" } --- $ sudo vi /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android.rules // [!code word:18d1] // [!code word:4ee7] // [!code ++] SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ATTR{idVendor}=="18d1", ATTR{idProduct}=="4ee7", MODE="0666", GROUP="plugdev" ``` After adding them, reload the udev rules and restart the service. ```sh { "title": "Reload udev rules" } --- $ sudo udevadm control --reload-rules $ sudo service udev restart ``` Now, connect via `adb shell` and check the image version. ```sh { "title": "Verify build version" } --- $ adb devices List of devices attached 4103e10fb64b2161 device $ adb root restarting adbd as root n5110:/# uname -a Linux localhost 3.0.101-lineage-gb7ffe7f2aea #2 SMP PREEMPT Fri Mar 6 14:25:02 KST 2026 armv7l n5110:/# getprop ro.build.display.id lineage_n5110-userdebug 7.1.2 NJH47F 91ef8e8628 test-keys ``` You can confirm that the system has booted normally with the custom-built image version. You can also verify the version information in the About tablet menu of the tablet UI. ### Conclusion The entire process, from image building to setting up the flashing environment, is now complete. Now you can modify the code as you study AOSP and apply it directly to the device. I will decide which parts to focus on analyzing and modifying after exploring the AOSP code a bit more.
